issues.legal_issue: Wrong legal advice, without moral delinquency, does not by itself constitute professional misconduct, although improper advice may do so.
material_facts: The disciplinary committee found that the advocates had given wrong legal advice on two matters, but also found that they had not cheated their clients.
The Court found considerable doubt that the conduct involved moral turpitude or moral delinquency.
issues.conclusion: Wrong legal advice or negligence alone, without moral delinquency, is not professional misconduct; improper advice may amount to professional misconduct in appropriate circumstances.
issues.legal_principle: Professional misconduct requires more than a mistake or negligence: moral delinquency must enter into the conduct. The Court relied on In re A Vakil, which followed In re G. Mayor Cooke, and noted that the approach had also been followed in In re An Advocate, the matter of An Advocate of Agra, and the matter of P. An Advocate. It distinguished improper advice from merely wrong advice and described an advocate's duties of good faith and protection of the client's interests.

predicates.advocates_disciplinary_proceeding: A professional disciplinary proceeding concerns an advocate's conduct in the practice of law.
predicates.wrong_advice_without_moral_delinquency: An advocate gives legal advice that is wrong, but the conduct is not shown to involve moral delinquency.

issues.definition: When a disciplinary proceeding concerns only wrong advice unaccompanied by moral delinquency, the advice alone does not amount to professional misconduct.

issues.legal_issue: A finding of professional misconduct cannot stand unless the charges are clearly established by convincing evidence rather than suspicion or conjecture.
material_facts: The clients who made an affidavit reciting that they had married verified its contents before a magistrate; the Court considered it likely that the recital had been made on their instructions, and found their oral evidence insufficient to rebut the circumstances supporting the affidavit.
In relation to another affidavit concerning a proposed gift of land, the elderly client could not identify who prepared it and unequivocally said that she had never approached the appellant for work.
The evidence and circumstances raised suspicion about the advocates' conduct, but did not establish the charged professional misconduct to the required standard.
issues.conclusion: The evidence fell short of the required proof of professional misconduct, so the disciplinary finding was set aside and the proceedings against the appellant were dropped.
issues.legal_principle: On an appeal under Section 38 of the Advocates Act, 1961, the Supreme Court generally does not disturb concurrent factual findings unless they rest on no evidence or on conjecture and surmise. Disciplinary charges require a higher degree of proof than in a civil suit but less than proof beyond reasonable doubt: there must be a convincing preponderance of evidence. Charges must be clearly proved and cannot be inferred from suspicion, however reasonable, or from error of judgment or indiscretion. The Court relied on A, a Pleader v. The Judges of the High Court of Madras and the professional-misconduct tests discussed in In re A Solicitor, Allinson v. General Council of Medical Education & Registration, George Frier Grahams v. Attorney General, and the matter of P. An Advocate.

predicates.disciplinary_appeal: An appeal challenges a finding made in an advocate's professional disciplinary proceeding.
predicates.evidence_does_not_convincingly_prove_pro: The evidence, including any circumstances raising suspicion, does not clearly and convincingly establish the charged professional misconduct.

issues.definition: In an appeal from a disciplinary finding, a finding is set aside when the evidence does not clearly and convincingly establish professional misconduct.
